country.comment: Trial conducted in rural villages across four provinces of the Democratic Republic of Congo: Kongo Central, Kasai, Kasai Central, and South Kivu (North Kivu was excluded prior to randomisation due to having only three clusters).

effect_estimate.comment: Primary and secondary outcomes were self-reported and analysed via linear intention-to-treat models with strata fixed effects and cluster-robust SEs. Text rounds secondary index effects to 1 decimal place (eg, 1.3 SDs for water governance, 0.6 SD for water satisfaction); Table 3 prints exact 2-decimal estimates. Subgroup effects varied significantly by province and remoteness (Tables 4-5).
effect_estimate.value: Intention-to-treat linear models (N = 1,312 households across 121 clusters, median 5 months post-intervention) found the VEA community-driven WASH and governance programme increased access to an improved primary water source by 33 percentage points (ITT 0.33, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.45; 83% intervention vs 43% control) and improved primary sanitation facility by 26 percentage points (ITT 0.26, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.37; 46% vs 18%), with no statistically significant overall effect on time spent collecting water (-3.0 min, 95% CI -19.7 to 13.6) or water quantity collected (+2.3 L, 95% CI -4.2 to 8.7). Among secondary outcomes, VEA increased the village-level water governance index (N = 328 villages) by 1.33 SD (95% CI 1.12 to 1.54), household water satisfaction index by 0.64 SD (95% CI 0.43 to 0.85), handwashing practices index by 0.48 SD (95% CI 0.25 to 0.71), and sanitation practices index by 0.28 SD (95% CI 0.12 to 0.44), with no significant effect on the financial cost of water index (+0.13 SD, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.36) or village-level water quality and access index (+0.13 SD, 95% CI -0.18 to 0.44).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 6-7, Results (Primary outcomes; Secondary outcomes), Table 2, and Table 3

mechanism_certainty.comment: Pre-registered cluster-randomised controlled trial (AEARCTR-0004648) appraised with RoB 2 that experimentally assigned the community-driven VEA programme and directly measured impacts on village water governance (+1.33 SD) and improved water/sanitation access (+33 pp / +26 pp). Note that VEA bundles participatory governance, Health Zone bureaucratic support, and Healthy Village certification with village infrastructure grants (approx. US$4,000/village for water and sanitation infrastructure), so the governance mechanism is not experimentally isolated from infrastructure financing, and outcomes are self-reported by unblinded respondents.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 3-5, Methods; PDF p. 6-7, Results, Tables 2-3; PDF p. 9, Discussion

mechanism_flags.comment: VEA operates through community-driven participation (collective community decision to request entry, participatory action planning, election and gender composition of a village WASH committee), bureaucratic assistance from Health Zone and Health Area officials (3-6 months of NGO/government support, volunteer training, monthly/weekly supervisory visits, co-developed maintenance plans), a 9-step administrative protocol (formal request, signed Health Zone agreement, baseline/follow-up evaluations, Chief Medical Officer inspection and Healthy Village certification), and village water user payments/financing (financial cost of water index and petty cash management training).

mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF p. 4-5, Methods (Intervention; Outcomes); PDF p. 7, Table 3; PDF p. 9, Discussion

outcome_flags.comment: Primary outcomes measured household use of an improved drinking water source and collection time (water_access), household use of an improved sanitation facility (sanitation_access), and litres of water collected per day (service_quantity). Secondary outcomes measured household payment for water via the financial cost of water index (affordability) and the village-level water quality and access / functional improved water points index (service_quality), alongside water governance and water satisfaction indices.
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 4-5, Methods (Outcomes); PDF p. 6-7, Results, Table 2, and Table 3

sample_size.comment: 332 eligible villages were grouped into 121 clusters; after 7 villages were randomly dropped to meet operational targets (note minor arithmetic difference in text: 332 minus 4 = 328 surveyed villages: 145 treatment + 183 control), 4 households per village were surveyed (1,312 households total). School attendance index had N = 1,260 households (558 intervention, 702 control); child health index had N = 1,388 children (646 intervention, 742 control); village-level indices had N = 328 villages.
sample_size.value: 1,312 households (580 intervention, 732 control) across 328 surveyed villages (145 intervention, 183 control; from 332 initial sample villages) in 121 clusters (50 treatment, 71 control) across 4 provinces; plus 328 village-level leadership surveys and 1,388 children aged 10-59 months (child health outcome)

study_design.value: Cluster-randomised controlled trial (stratified by province and number of villages per cluster; intention-to-treat linear regression analysis)
